title: Metric TSP subtour-relaxation gap
subfield: Routing, network optimization, and mathematical foundations
open: Prove or disprove that the subtour-elimination linear programming relaxation of the symmetric metric traveling salesman problem has integrality gap exactly \(4/3\).
status: Decades old. Exact computations reported in 2026 extend verification through 15 vertices; finite verification does not settle arbitrary instances.
why: Would sharpen a foundational lower bound used in routing optimization.
key_works: Cook, Hougardy, and Petrich (2026), *Extending Exact Integrality Gap Computations for the Metric TSP*, arXiv:2603.12995.

title: A general \(4/3\)-approximation for metric TSP
subfield: Routing, network optimization, and mathematical foundations
open: Construct a polynomial-time algorithm returning a tour of cost at most \(4/3\) of optimum for every symmetric metric instance.
status: Better-than-\(3/2\) approximation is established, but does not approach the conjectured \(4/3\) guarantee.
why: Would improve worst-case guarantees for distribution, inspection, and service routing.
key_works: Karlin, Klein, and Oveis Gharan (2023), *A deterministic better-than-3/2 approximation algorithm for metric TSP*, DOI:10.1007/978-3-031-32726-1_19; Cook et al. (2026), arXiv:2603.12995.

title: The general half-integral TSP frontier
subfield: Routing, network optimization, and mathematical foundations
open: Obtain a \(4/3\)-approximation for all metric TSP instances with an optimal half-integral subtour solution, beyond presently tractable structural subclasses.
status: A 2025 result achieves \(4/3\) for half-integral cycle-cut instances; the unrestricted half-integral case is broader.
why: Could isolate the combinatorial obstruction behind the general TSP conjecture.
key_works: Jin, Klein, and Williamson (2025), *A 4/3-approximation algorithm for half-integral cycle cut instances of the TSP*, DOI:10.1007/s10107-025-02193-5.

title: Variance of random Euclidean tour length
subfield: Routing, network optimization, and mathematical foundations
open: Determine the finite-size and asymptotic variance of optimal tours through uniformly sampled points in a disc.
status: Leading tour-length scaling is classical; the variance question was explicitly posed at Dagstuhl in 2024.
why: Would quantify uncertainty in spatial logistics approximations.
key_works: Beardwood, Halton, and Hammersley (1959), *The shortest path through many points*; Connors, in Correa et al. (2025), *Dynamic Traffic Models in Transportation Science*, §4.2.

title: A three-approximation for unsplittable capacitated routing
subfield: Routing, network optimization, and mathematical foundations
open: Find a polynomial-time 3-approximation for general metric unsplittable capacitated vehicle routing, or establish a stronger approximation barrier.
status: Zhao and Xiao report ratios below 3.1759 for variable capacity and below 3.0897 for fixed capacity in 2026.
why: Addresses indivisible deliveries whose demands cannot be divided among vehicles.
key_works: Zhao and Xiao (2026), *Improved Approximations for the Unsplittable Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem*, arXiv:2601.21660.

title: Tight approximation for capacitated arc routing
subfield: Routing, network optimization, and mathematical foundations
open: Close the approximation gap for undirected unit-demand capacitated arc routing; a concrete target is a uniform 2-approximation.
status: A 2025 algorithm improves the longstanding bound to \(5/2-\Theta(1/\sqrt{k})\), where \(k\) is vehicle capacity.
why: Applies to waste collection, street inspection, sweeping, and winter maintenance.
key_works: Zhao and Xiao (2025), *An Improved Approximation Algorithm for the Capacitated Arc Routing Problem*, arXiv:2508.05471.

title: Multiple-depot capacitated routing below four
subfield: Routing, network optimization, and mathematical foundations
open: Determine the tight approximation threshold for metric multiple-depot, unit-demand capacitated routing; a useful next target is a factor of 3.
status: Friggstad and Mömke obtain a 3.9365-approximation in their 2025 work.
why: Joint depot assignment and routing remain harder than solving independent depot territories.
key_works: Friggstad and Mömke (2025), *Approximating Multiple-Depot Capacitated Vehicle Routing via LP Rounding*, arXiv:2510.05321.

title: Railway Convoy Conjecture
subfield: Routing, network optimization, and mathematical foundations
open: In the directed acyclic network model with common origin, destination, travel times, and minimum entry headway, prove that an optimal makespan solution always uses identical or disjoint train paths.
status: Established for three trains; explicitly open for four or more.
why: Could eliminate intermediate waiting from optimal solutions.
key_works: Eickhoff, in Correa et al. (2025), *Dynamic Traffic Models in Transportation Science*, §4.3.

title: Dynamic routing games with heterogeneous deadlines
subfield: Routing, network optimization, and mathematical foundations
open: Characterize equilibrium existence and inefficiency when travelers have different deadlines and lateness penalties.
status: Deadline-based bicriteria models have partial theory; heterogeneous deadlines remain an explicitly identified extension.
why: Represents deliveries and appointments more realistically than travel-time-only objectives.
key_works: Oosterwijk, Schmand, and Schröder (2024), *Bicriteria Nash Flows over Time*, DOI:10.1016/j.geb.2024.06.002; Dagstuhl 24281, §4.1.

title: Coupled traffic–charging–electricity equilibrium
subfield: Routing, network optimization, and mathematical foundations
open: Establish existence conditions and convergent algorithms when route choice, finite charging queues, battery feasibility, and distribution-grid constraints jointly determine feasible travel.
status: Dynamic energy-feasible traffic equilibria are established in restricted models; endogenous charging-power and queue feedback introduce additional coupling.
why: Prevents traffic plans and electricity plans from assuming mutually incompatible behavior.
key_works: Graf, Harks, and Palkar (2022), *Dynamic Traffic Assignment for Electric Vehicles*, arXiv:2207.04454.

title: Causal mechanism of capacity drop
open: Design field experiments that distinguish competing explanations of discharge-flow reduction after congestion begins, rather than merely fitting the same aggregate curve.
status: Models reproduce capacity drop, but matching observations does not uniquely identify the responsible behavioral mechanism.
why: Different mechanisms imply different effective controls.
key_works: Treiber, Kesting, and Helbing (2006), *Understanding widely scattered traffic flows, the capacity drop, platoons, and times-to-collision as effects of variance-driven time gaps*, DOI:10.1103/PhysRevE.74.016123.

title: Predictive distribution of traffic breakdown
open: Produce calibrated probabilities for the time and location of congestion onset, conditional on demand, vehicle composition, weather, and recent disturbances.
status: Stochastic and behavioral models explain variability; transferable, intervention-sensitive breakdown probabilities remain a forecasting target.
why: Enables preventive control before queues form.
key_works: Treiber, Kesting, and Helbing (2006), *Understanding widely scattered traffic flows…*, DOI:10.1103/PhysRevE.74.016123.

title: String stability with changing vehicle order
open: Guarantee bounded disturbance amplification when heterogeneous vehicles repeatedly join, leave, and cut into a platoon, with actuator limits and uncertain human responses.
status: Strong safety and stability results exist under specified dynamics; arbitrary switching and real cut-in behavior exceed many assumptions.
why: Prevents local cruise-control improvements from amplifying downstream braking.
key_works: Berger et al. (2026), *String stability and guaranteed safety via funnel cruise control*.

title: Transferable urban macroscopic fundamental diagrams
open: Identify observable conditions under which an aggregate flow–accumulation relationship transfers across days, neighborhoods, and interventions without complete recalibration.
status: Urban-scale relationships have been measured since 2008; their portability depends on network structure and congestion distribution.
why: Supports citywide control using fewer state variables.
key_works: Geroliminis and Daganzo (2008), *Existence of urban-scale macroscopic fundamental diagrams: Some experimental findings*; Wang et al. (2015), *An Empirical Analysis of Macroscopic Fundamental Diagrams for Sendai Road Networks*.

title: Adaptive congestion-region partitioning
open: Partition a city into regions whose aggregate traffic dynamics remain identifiable as congestion boundaries move, while preventing unstable repartitioning.
status: Dynamic clustering methods exist; predictive validity and closed-loop guarantees under changing partitions remain separate requirements.
why: Fixed administrative zones often poorly represent moving queues.
key_works: Saeedmanesh and Geroliminis (2017), *Dynamic clustering and propagation of congestion in heterogeneously congested urban traffic networks*.

title: Causal interpretation of network hysteresis
open: Separate the effects of spatial congestion patterns, route changes, measurement aggregation, and demand history on hysteresis in network flow–accumulation diagrams.
status: Hysteresis is observed and modeled; the same aggregate loop can conceal different internal states.
why: Determines whether a controller can safely act on accumulation alone.
key_works: Wang, Wada, Akamatsu, and Hara (2015), *An Empirical Analysis of Macroscopic Fundamental Diagrams for Sendai Road Networks*.

title: Computable spillback equilibria at metropolitan scale
open: Develop scalable equilibrium algorithms with certified residuals for dynamic networks containing finite storage, spillback, and realistic junction interactions.
status: Equilibrium existence with spillback is not wholly open; computational scalability and stronger operational models remain distinct gaps.
why: Point-queue approximations can miss gridlock and upstream blocking.
key_works: Sering and Vargas Koch (2018), *Nash Flows over Time with Spillback and Kinematic Waves*, arXiv:1807.05862.

title: Day-to-day learning without unstable route oscillation
open: Find empirically defensible traveler-learning rules that converge, or characterize their persistent oscillations, when information is delayed, incomplete, and shared strategically.
status: Bounded-rationality and information-sharing models have been simulated; convergence and behavioral identification are model-dependent.
why: Navigation systems can create synchronized rerouting rather than equilibrium.
key_works: Yu, Han, and Ochieng (2018), *Day-to-Day Dynamic Traffic Assignment with Imperfect Information, Bounded Rationality and Information Sharing*, arXiv:1811.10729.

title: Driver-model parameters under intervention
open: Identify which car-following and route-learning parameters remain invariant after pricing, automation, road redesign, or information changes.
status: Successful observational calibration does not establish that fitted parameters survive interventions.
why: Policy simulations fail when behavior changes precisely because a policy is introduced.
key_works: Yu, Han, and Ochieng (2018), *Day-to-Day Dynamic Traffic Assignment…*; Treiber et al. (2006), DOI:10.1103/PhysRevE.74.016123.

title: Long-run rebound from traffic smoothing
open: Measure whether smoother traffic reduces total energy and delay after travelers adjust departure times, routes, destinations, and trip frequency.
status: Large field demonstrations address immediate traffic dynamics; long-run demand responses require different experimental designs.
why: Short-run fuel savings need not equal persistent systemwide savings.
key_works: Ameli et al. (2024), *Designing, simulating, and performing the 100-AV field test for the CIRCLES consortium*, arXiv:2404.15533; Duranton and Turner (2011), DOI:10.1257/aer.101.6.2616.

title: Minimum effective penetration of traffic-smoothing vehicles
open: Determine the smallest controllable vehicle share that reliably suppresses disturbances across specified road geometries, demand regimes, and human-driver populations.
status: A single controlled vehicle damped waves in ring experiments; this is not a universal penetration threshold.
why: Sets realistic deployment requirements for partial automation.
key_works: Stern et al. (2018), *Dissipation of stop-and-go waves via control of autonomous vehicles: Field experiments*, DOI:10.1016/j.trc.2018.02.005.

title: Replicable open-road smoothing benefits
open: Replicate controlled-vehicle effects across independent freeway sites using preregistered energy, safety, and throughput endpoints.
status: CIRCLES implemented a 100-vehicle field experiment; broader geographic and operational replication is a separate evidence requirement.
why: Distinguishes deployable benefits from site-specific demonstration effects.
key_works: Ameli et al. (2024), *Designing, simulating, and performing the 100-AV field test for the CIRCLES consortium*, arXiv:2404.15533.

title: Safe platooning through communication outages
open: Maintain collision avoidance and acceptable disturbance amplification through burst packet loss, delayed messages, and transitions between cooperative and independent control.
status: Guaranteed controllers exist for specified sensing and dynamics; realistic communication faults require integrated certification.
why: Communication failure must not trigger coordinated unsafe braking.
key_works: Berger et al. (2026), *String stability and guaranteed safety via funnel cruise control*.

title: Spillback-safe multimodal max-pressure control
open: Combine finite road storage, pedestrian clearance, transit priority, and changing turning fractions while preserving a meaningful network-stability guarantee.
status: Capacity-aware backpressure addresses important finite-buffer limitations; the combined multimodal guarantee remains the stronger target.
why: Vehicle-throughput optimization alone can starve pedestrians or block neighboring intersections.
key_works: Gregoire et al., *Capacity-aware backpressure traffic signal control*, DOI:10.1109/TCNS.2014.2378871.

title: Traffic control with unobservable queues
open: Infer actionable queue states from sparse, biased connected-vehicle or crowdsourced observations, with explicit uncertainty propagated into signal decisions.
status: Delay-based crowdsourced control has been demonstrated; missing users and changing sampling rates remain important observability problems.
why: Most intersections cannot assume complete, reliable vehicle detection.
key_works: Dixit et al. (2020), *A simple crowdsourced delay-based traffic signal control*.

title: Safe transfer of learned signal controllers
open: Transfer a learned controller to a new network without allowing exploratory actions to violate safety constraints or destabilize queues.
status: A 2026 study demonstrates parameter-sharing transfer to larger corridor networks; arbitrary network and demand shifts remain broader targets.
why: Retraining every city from scratch limits practical deployment.
key_works: Song, Eder, Lawry, and Wilson (2026), *Systematic Analyses of Reinforcement Learning Controllers in Signalized Urban Corridors*, arXiv:2604.02025.

title: Certified capacity regions for learned traffic control
open: Compute defensible inner and outer bounds on the demand vectors a learned signal controller can stabilize, rather than reporting average delay on selected scenarios.
status: Capacity-region evaluation has been developed for corridor experiments; certification for large uncertain networks remains a target.
why: Reveals catastrophic overload regions hidden by average performance.
key_works: Song et al. (2026), *Systematic Analyses of Reinforcement Learning Controllers in Signalized Urban Corridors*, arXiv:2604.02025.

title: Conditions for emergent green waves
open: Explain when decentralized controllers produce persistent progression bands, and when local optimization instead creates unstable coordination.
status: Initial 2026 results suggest spontaneous green waves under parameter sharing; general conditions are not established by those experiments.
why: Could enable coordination without expensive centralized optimization.
key_works: Song et al. (2026), *Systematic Analyses of Reinforcement Learning Controllers in Signalized Urban Corridors*, arXiv:2604.02025.

title: Joint freeway–urban perimeter control
open: Coordinate freeway access, urban boundary inflows, and internal signals without merely relocating queues to another network or jurisdiction.
status: Regional macroscopic control and freeway models exist; their joint spillback-aware operation requires stronger coupled models and field evidence.
why: Freeway and arterial congestion cannot always be optimized independently.
key_works: Geroliminis and Daganzo (2008), *Existence of urban-scale macroscopic fundamental diagrams*; Cassidy et al. (2011), *Macroscopic Fundamental Diagrams for Freeway Networks*, DOI:10.3141/2260-02.

title: Auditable priority among conflicting road users
open: Design real-time priority rules for emergency vehicles, buses, pedestrians, and ordinary traffic with explicit bounds on the delay and risk imposed on each group.
status: Individual priority mechanisms exist; jointly auditable guarantees are a proposed system-level target.
why: “Priority” becomes ambiguous when several justified priorities conflict.
key_works: Gregoire et al., *Capacity-aware backpressure traffic signal control*; Guihaire and Hao (2008), *Transit network design and scheduling: A global review*.

title: Context-dependent induced-demand elasticities
subfield: Travel behavior, land use, and transport economics
open: Identify how induced travel varies with initial congestion, land supply, road type, pricing, and development restrictions.
status: Induced demand is established; a single estimated elasticity does not automatically transfer between settings.
why: Improves forecasts of road expansion’s congestion and emissions consequences.
key_works: Duranton and Turner (2011), *The Fundamental Law of Road Congestion: Evidence from US Cities*, DOI:10.1257/aer.101.6.2616.

title: Welfare from capacity expansion beyond travel-time savings
subfield: Travel behavior, land use, and transport economics
open: Estimate road expansion’s general-equilibrium welfare effects, including new activities, relocation, freight productivity, pollution, and distributional changes.
status: Evidence that traffic expands with roads does not itself determine whether a particular project increases welfare.
why: Avoids equating either congestion relief or induced traffic with the complete social outcome.
key_works: Duranton and Turner (2011), *The Fundamental Law of Road Congestion*, DOI:10.1257/aer.101.6.2616.

title: Telework’s household-wide travel rebound
subfield: Travel behavior, land use, and transport economics
open: Measure total household travel and emissions after telework changes residential location, nonwork trips, vehicle ownership, and other household members’ behavior.
status: Studies document context-dependent effects; avoided commuting alone is an incomplete endpoint.
why: Determines whether remote work is an effective transportation decarbonization measure.
key_works: Cerqueira et al. (2020), *Does working from home reduce CO2 emissions? An analysis of travel patterns as dictated by workplaces*, DOI:10.1016/j.trd.2020.102338.

title: Built environment versus residential self-selection
subfield: Travel behavior, land use, and transport economics
open: Identify the causal effect of neighborhood design on travel while separating people’s prior preferences, housing constraints, and relocation decisions.
status: Correlations are abundant; transportable causal estimates remain a central land-use research need.
why: Determines which urban-design interventions actually change behavior.
key_works: National Academies (2024), *Critical Issues in Transportation for 2024 and Beyond*, “Land Use,” DOI:10.17226/27432.

title: A sufficient-accessibility threshold
subfield: Travel behavior, land use, and transport economics
open: Define and validate the level of access to jobs, care, education, and social activity required for households to thrive, accounting for individual constraints.
status: Accessibility measures exist; a defensible sufficiency threshold is explicitly identified as unresolved.
why: Replaces “more mobility is always better” with an outcome-based standard.
key_works: National Academies (2024), *Critical Issues in Transportation for 2024 and Beyond*, “Promoting Equity and Inclusion.”

title: Accessibility gains without displacement
subfield: Travel behavior, land use, and transport economics
open: Design transport-and-housing interventions that improve access for existing residents without pricing those residents out of the improved area.
status: Coordinating land use and transport remains an identified governance and research problem; project-level gains can conceal population replacement.
why: Prevents accessibility investments from relocating their intended beneficiaries.
key_works: National Academies (2024), *Critical Issues in Transportation for 2024 and Beyond*, “Land Use.”

title: Perceived danger versus experienced harassment
subfield: Travel behavior, land use, and transport economics
open: Identify how actual harassment risk, perceived risk, social restrictions, and avoidance behavior separately constrain travel choices.
status: Research links perceived street risk to consequential educational decisions; distinguishing mechanisms remains essential for intervention design.
why: Recorded incidents miss trips never attempted.
key_works: Borker (2021), *Safety First: Perceived Risk of Street Harassment and Educational Choices of Women*, World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 9731.

title: Politically durable mode-shift packages
subfield: Travel behavior, land use, and transport economics
open: Identify combinations of service improvements, street redesign, pricing, and compensation that produce substantial sustained mode shift without requiring politically unattainable assumptions.
status: The National Academies’ 2024 research agenda explicitly asks how large mode shifts can be achieved without steep fuel or carbon taxes.
why: Technically efficient policies are ineffective when repeatedly reversed.
key_works: National Academies (2024), *Critical Issues in Transportation for 2024 and Beyond*, research appendix.

title: Harassment interventions that expand feasible opportunities
subfield: Travel behavior, land use, and transport economics
open: Test whether interventions increase the destinations and activities women can actually choose, rather than merely improving reported comfort among existing riders.
status: Opportunity costs of perceived danger have been measured; comparative causal evidence on remedies remains the target.
why: Connects transportation safety to education and employment outcomes.
key_works: Borker (2021), *Safety First: Perceived Risk of Street Harassment and Educational Choices of Women*, Working Paper 9731.

title: Endogenous platform-driver labor supply
subfield: Travel behavior, land use, and transport economics
open: Model and validate how drivers jointly respond to fares, waiting time, work flexibility, expenses, and competing platforms.
status: The value of flexible work has been estimated; stable policy predictions require richer endogenous participation and multi-platform behavior.
why: Dispatch and pricing models often treat available labor as an external input.
key_works: Chen, Chevalier, Rossi, and Oehlsen (2019), *The Value of Flexible Work: Evidence from Uber Drivers*, DOI:10.1086/702171.

title: Causal safety in numbers
open: Determine how much lower per-person collision risk comes from driver adaptation, infrastructure change, route selection, or other confounding factors.
status: The association is longstanding; its causal decomposition and transferability are not supplied by the original observational relationship.
why: Changes the predicted safety consequences of increasing walking or cycling.
key_works: Jacobsen (2003), *Safety in numbers: more walkers and bicyclists, safer walking and bicycling*, DOI:10.1136/ip.9.3.205.

title: Exposure denominators for small mobility modes
open: Measure distance, time, trips, and interaction exposure for cycling, scooters, wheelchairs, and walking with comparable uncertainty estimates.
status: Micromobility safety assessments identify inconsistent exposure and injury data as obstacles to comparisons.
why: Injury counts alone cannot establish whether one mode or intervention is safer.
key_works: Yannis, Crist, and Petraki (2024), *Safer micromobility: technical background report*; ITF (2024), *Safer Micromobility*.

title: Transferable crossing-treatment effects
open: Predict which crossing interventions work at a new location given vehicle speeds, pedestrian populations, visibility, turning movements, and compliance.
status: Pedestrian hybrid beacons are an established countermeasure; reliable local treatment-effect prediction is a stronger requirement.
why: Supports effective retrofits rather than uniform installation rules.
key_works: FHWA, *Pedestrian Hybrid Beacons*, Proven Safety Countermeasures program.

title: Micromobility geometry and injury severity
open: Establish validated relationships between wheel size, steering geometry, braking, rider posture, and injury outcomes across real road defects.
status: Vehicle-design recommendations exist; comparable crash and near-crash evidence across designs remains limited.
why: Could reduce injuries without relying solely on rider behavior.
key_works: ITF (2024), *Safer Micromobility*, DOI:10.1787/0d2e0dd5-en.

title: Nighttime micromobility conspicuity
open: Determine lighting and conspicuity designs that improve detection and correct speed judgment without glare or misleading visual cues.
status: Safety guidance addresses visibility; performance across road layouts, weather, and rider populations remains an experimental target.
why: Being noticed is not equivalent to being perceived accurately.
key_works: ITF (2024), *Safer Micromobility*, DOI:10.1787/0d2e0dd5-en.

title: Micromobility near-miss metrics that predict injury
open: Validate whether video-derived conflict indicators predict future serious injuries across different micromobility modes and street designs.
status: Surrogate indicators offer faster feedback than crash counts, but require mode-specific validation.
why: Prevents optimizing a convenient proxy that does not track harm.
key_works: Yannis, Crist, and Petraki (2024), *Safer micromobility: technical background report*.

title: Transient sidewalk obstruction mapping
open: Detect temporary barriers—including parked scooters, construction, deliveries, and snow—and update accessible routes before travelers encounter them.
status: Large-scale accessibility inventories exist; transient conditions are harder than persistent curb and pavement defects.
why: A nominally accessible route can become unusable within minutes.
key_works: Saha et al. (2019), *Project Sidewalk: A Web-based Crowdsourcing Tool for Collecting Sidewalk Accessibility Data at Scale*, DOI:10.1145/3290605.3300292.

title: Marginal value of a missing active-travel link
open: Estimate how completing a specific network gap changes participation and risk, including trips that were previously suppressed.
status: Network-wide exposure and safety relationships are known; individual-link effects are nonlinear and context-dependent.
why: A short connection can matter more than a much longer disconnected facility.
key_works: Jacobsen (2003), *Safety in numbers: more walkers and bicyclists, safer walking and bicycling*.

title: Micromobility’s true displaced mode
open: Measure the counterfactual trip replaced by shared micromobility, including walking, public transport, private cars, and trips that would not otherwise occur.
status: Lifecycle analyses show sensitivity to use patterns and alternatives; substitution varies by place and user.
why: Determines whether deployment reduces emissions and congestion.
key_works: Hollingsworth, Copeland, and Johnson (2019), *Are e-scooters polluters? The environmental impacts of shared dockless electric scooters*, DOI:10.1088/1748-9326/ab2da8.

title: Tenfold longer useful micromobility service
open: As a proposed moonshot, increase useful passenger-kilometers per manufactured shared scooter tenfold against a specified baseline without shifting burdens into maintenance or collection.
status: Lifecycle work identifies manufacturing and fleet servicing as important contributors; the target requires whole-system validation.
why: Durability may outperform incremental battery-efficiency improvements.
key_works: Hollingsworth, Copeland, and Johnson (2019), *Are e-scooters polluters?*, DOI:10.1088/1748-9326/ab2da8.

title: Reliability of the complete accessible journey
subfield: Accessibility, disability, and complete trip chains
open: Predict whether an entire trip remains feasible when sidewalks, elevators, vehicles, boarding interfaces, and assistance services can each fail.
status: Accessibility inventories address individual barriers; end-to-end reliability requires their dependencies and changing states.
why: One failed segment can invalidate every otherwise accessible component.
key_works: Saha et al. (2019), *Project Sidewalk*, DOI:10.1145/3290605.3300292.

title: Uncertainty-aware accessibility attributes
subfield: Accessibility, disability, and complete trip chains
open: Attach calibrated uncertainty to sidewalk slope, width, curb condition, surface quality, and obstruction labels, then propagate it into route recommendations.
status: Large image galleries and crowdsourced labels exist; uncertainty must be meaningful to users with different tolerances.
why: Incorrectly confident accessibility information can strand travelers.
key_works: Duan et al. (2021), *Sidewalk Gallery: An Interactive, Filterable Image Gallery of Over 500,000 Sidewalk Accessibility Problems*.

title: Turning accessibility reports into repairs
subfield: Accessibility, disability, and complete trip chains
open: Determine institutional and funding arrangements that reliably convert reported barriers into verified repairs, without favoring neighborhoods with more reporting capacity.
status: Accessibility has been analyzed as a sociopolitical problem; data collection alone does not establish effective remediation.
why: An accurate map of barriers is not the same as an accessible city.
key_works: Saha et al. (2020), *Urban Accessibility as a Socio-Political Problem: A Multi-Stakeholder Analysis*.

title: Wheelchairs as certified aircraft seats
subfield: Accessibility, disability, and complete trip chains
open: Demonstrate crashworthy wheelchair-and-restraint configurations across a representative range of chairs, occupants, and aircraft loading conditions.
status: A 2021 assessment found technical feasibility worth pursuing; feasibility is not universal certification.
why: Could eliminate dangerous transfers and damage to essential mobility equipment.
key_works: National Academies (2021), *Technical Feasibility of a Wheelchair Securement Concept for Airline Travel: A Preliminary Assessment*, DOI:10.17226/26323.

title: Interoperable aircraft wheelchair securement
subfield: Accessibility, disability, and complete trip chains
open: Develop an interface that safely accommodates diverse wheelchairs without requiring each chair–aircraft combination to become a bespoke installation.
status: Securement concepts exist; compatibility, loading, and operational integration remain broader engineering requirements.
why: A technically safe niche configuration may still be unusable at fleet scale.
key_works: National Academies (2021), *Technical Feasibility of a Wheelchair Securement Concept for Airline Travel*, DOI:10.17226/26323.

title: Wheelchair-inclusive aircraft emergency procedures
subfield: Accessibility, disability, and complete trip chains
open: Validate evacuation and emergency-response procedures for passengers remaining in their wheelchairs, including constrained aisles and unavailable assistance.
status: Preliminary feasibility work does not close all operational and emergency integration questions.
why: Accessibility must remain safe outside normal boarding and cruising.
key_works: National Academies (2021), *Technical Feasibility of a Wheelchair Securement Concept for Airline Travel*, DOI:10.17226/26323.

title: Reliable dynamic paratransit insertion
subfield: Accessibility, disability, and complete trip chains
open: Insert new requests and handle cancellations while preserving individual ride-time, assistance, vehicle-compatibility, and appointment constraints.
status: Dial-a-ride optimization is mature in many formulations; robust real-time service across these combined constraints remains a deployment target.
why: Average efficiency can conceal unacceptable service for riders with complex needs.
key_works: Cordeau and Laporte (2007), *The dial-a-ride problem: models and algorithms*, DOI:10.1007/s10479-007-0170-8.

title: Recovery after an accessible connection fails
subfield: Accessibility, disability, and complete trip chains
open: Replan and actually deliver assistance when an elevator, vehicle, transfer, or booked support service fails, with a bound on abandonment and delay.
status: Route optimization and accessibility mapping provide components; coordinated recovery across operators is a stronger target.
why: Accessible travel requires dependable recovery, not just optimistic initial planning.
key_works: Cordeau and Laporte (2007), *The dial-a-ride problem*; Project Sidewalk research program.

title: Measuring disability-related suppressed travel
subfield: Accessibility, disability, and complete trip chains
open: Estimate trips and opportunities forgone because of disability-related barriers, distinguishing unmet demand from voluntary nontravel.
status: National travel surveys document realized travel differences; unrealized desired journeys are harder to observe.
why: Counting only completed trips understates exclusion.
key_works: Bureau of Transportation Statistics (2026 update), *Travel Patterns of American Adults with Disabilities*, using the 2022 National Household Travel Survey.

title: Cognitive accessibility of trip execution
subfield: Accessibility, disability, and complete trip chains
open: Validate booking, wayfinding, transfers, and disruption messages for people with differing cognitive, sensory, and communication needs, using independently completed journeys as the endpoint.
status: Aggregate disability travel statistics do not identify which interface changes close which execution barriers.
why: Physical accessibility alone does not make a trip independently usable.
key_works: Bureau of Transportation Statistics, *Travel Patterns of American Adults with Disabilities*, 2026 update.

title: Passenger-optimal bus-bunching control
open: Control headways while accounting for passengers already onboard, waiting passengers, crowding, and downstream transfers rather than optimizing headway regularity alone.
status: Headway-based anti-bunching control is established; passenger-level objectives introduce additional trade-offs.
why: Holding a bus can help future riders while harming current ones.
key_works: Daganzo (2009), *A headway-based approach to eliminate bus bunching: Systematic analysis and comparisons*.

title: Transfer-aware cooperation between buses
open: Coordinate holding across intersecting routes without causing cascading missed connections or destabilizing either route.
status: Bus-to-bus cooperation addresses bunching; network-wide transfer dependencies require broader coordination.
why: A locally regular route can still produce unreliable journeys.
key_works: Daganzo and Pilachowski (2011), *Reducing bunching with bus-to-bus cooperation*.

title: Bunching with denied boarding
open: Stabilize service when full vehicles leave passengers behind and the resulting queues alter later dwell times and boarding demand.
status: Classical holding analyses provide foundations; capacity saturation creates additional positive feedback.
why: The busiest services are often those least well represented by unconstrained boarding models.
key_works: Daganzo (2009), *A headway-based approach to eliminate bus bunching*.

title: Joint transit route, frequency, and timetable design
open: Solve city-scale design problems that jointly choose routes, frequencies, and timetables while representing passenger reassignment and uncertainty.
status: Extensive decomposition and optimization methods exist; integration, scale, and realistic behavior remain competing demands.
why: Independently optimized planning stages can undo one another’s benefits.
key_works: Guihaire and Hao (2008), *Transit network design and scheduling: A global review*, DOI:10.1016/j.tra.2008.03.011.

title: Service guarantees for pooled demand-responsive transit
open: Determine achievable trade-offs between vehicle productivity, maximum wait, detour, rejection probability, and equitable coverage under uncertain requests.
status: Dial-a-ride algorithms address many variants; universally favorable pooling claims are not supported without demand and service assumptions.
why: Clarifies when pooling is genuinely useful rather than merely cheap for the operator.
key_works: Cordeau and Laporte (2007), *The dial-a-ride problem: models and algorithms*.

title: Fixed-route versus flexible-service transition thresholds
open: Identify empirically validated demand-density and variability thresholds for switching among fixed routes, feeders, and demand-responsive service.
status: Transit design methods provide alternatives, but thresholds depend on geography, service guarantees, and endogenous demand.
why: Avoids replacing productive buses with inefficient small vehicles, or running nearly empty fixed routes indefinitely.
key_works: Guihaire and Hao (2008), *Transit network design and scheduling: A global review*.

title: Integrated electric-bus scheduling under disruption
open: Jointly recover timetables, vehicle assignments, charging, and driver duties after delays or charger failures while preserving passenger service.
status: Integrated timetabling and vehicle scheduling has been demonstrated; electrification adds energy and infrastructure dependencies.
why: A feasible timetable is useless when assigned vehicles cannot charge or drivers cannot legally operate it.
key_works: Ibarra-Rojas, Giesen, and Rios-Solis (2014), *An integrated approach for timetabling and vehicle scheduling problems to analyze the trade-off between level of service and operating costs of transit networks*.

title: Incentive-compatible through-ticketing
open: Design fare integration and revenue-sharing arrangements that reward reliable transfers and coverage without encouraging operators to reject unprofitable connecting passengers.
status: Integrated ticketing exists; aligned incentives across independent operators remain a governance problem.
why: Payment interoperability alone does not create an integrated service.
key_works: National Academies (2024), *Critical Issues in Transportation for 2024 and Beyond*, “Governance.”

title: Stable funding for useful transit operations
open: Establish funding mechanisms that sustain useful frequency and maintenance through demand shocks rather than disproportionately favoring new capital projects.
status: The mismatch between operating needs and available funding remains an identified institutional problem.
why: Infrastructure delivers little value without dependable service.
key_works: National Academies (2024), *Critical Issues in Transportation for 2024 and Beyond*, “Funding and Finance.”

title: Transit rosters that retain workers
open: Quantify and optimize the effects of split shifts, schedule predictability, recovery time, and route assignments on retention and service reliability.
status: Workforce shortages and skill needs are documented; causal evidence on the best operational remedies remains incomplete.
why: Nominal fleet capacity does not become service without a sustainable workforce.
key_works: National Academies (2024), *Critical Issues in Transportation for 2024 and Beyond*, “Workforce.”

title: Certifiable virtual coupling
open: Establish a certifiable operating envelope for trains following more closely through coordinated braking, including communication faults and heterogeneous equipment.
status: Reviews through 2026 describe substantial control development; deployment requires integration with safety assurance and railway operations.
why: Could increase capacity without constructing equivalent additional track.
key_works: Félez and Vaquero-Serrano (2023), *Virtual Coupling in Railways: A Comprehensive Review*, DOI:10.3390/machines11050521; Zhang et al. (2026), DOI:10.1007/s40864-026-00277-9.

title: Virtual coupling through junctions
open: Safely form, split, and reroute virtual train groups around switches and stations without erasing their headway advantage.
status: Following control is only one component; topology-changing operations require additional coordination and verification.
why: Railway capacity is often constrained by junctions rather than plain track.
key_works: Zhang et al. (2026), *A Comprehensive Review of Virtually Coupled Train Systems*, DOI:10.1007/s40864-026-00277-9.

title: Heterogeneous braking in closely spaced trains
open: Account for load, adhesion, brake degradation, and uncertain response times when certifying safe following distances between unlike trains.
status: Robust control approaches exist; dependable bounds for heterogeneous operational fleets remain a demanding target.
why: A following train cannot assume the leader shares its braking capabilities.
key_works: Félez and Vaquero-Serrano (2023), *Virtual Coupling in Railways: A Comprehensive Review*.

title: Local low-adhesion forecasting
open: Forecast short-lived low-adhesion patches at braking-relevant spatial and temporal resolution before trains encounter them.
status: Adhesion research remains an active railway program; localized contamination and weather make network-wide prediction difficult.
why: Improves both braking safety and timetable reliability.
key_works: RSSB, *Adhesion Research Group* research program.

title: Wheel–rail friction under thin contamination layers
open: Predict and reproduce friction transitions caused by small quantities of water and mixed contaminants across load, speed, and surface histories.
status: Full-scale experiments demonstrate important low-adhesion effects; general predictive friction maps remain the target.
why: Small environmental changes can produce disproportionately large braking changes.
key_works: Buckley-Johnstone et al. (2020), *Full-scale testing of low adhesion effects with small amounts of water in the wheel/rail interface*.

title: Non-destructive ballast moisture and fouling inference
open: Infer subsurface fouling and retained water from affordable inspections across seasons, ballast types, and track structures.
status: Infrared thermography and statistical processing have shown promise; transfer across field conditions requires validation.
why: Hidden deterioration affects drainage, settlement, and maintenance needs.
key_works: Koohmishi, Gao, Jing, and Guo (2025), *Non-destructive assessment of railway ballast fouling and water retention using infrared thermography and statistical processing*, DOI:10.1016/j.conbuildmat.2025.140273.

title: Causal prediction of tamping benefit
open: Predict not only when track geometry will deteriorate, but how each feasible tamping intervention changes future deterioration and total maintenance demand.
status: Models predict future tamping requirements; intervention-effect identification is a stronger requirement than forecasting untreated trends.
why: Repeated maintenance can alter the material whose behavior is being predicted.
key_works: Charoenwong et al. (2025), *Prediction of future railway ballast tamping requirements*, Transportation Geotechnics 55, 101652.

title: Transferable corrugation-maintenance selection
open: Choose durable, cost-effective combinations of grinding, friction management, and vehicle–track changes across different corrugation mechanisms.
status: Corrugation mechanisms and treatments are extensively understood; the open target is transferable lifecycle intervention selection, not explaining corrugation from scratch.
why: Repeatedly removing damage without changing its cause wastes maintenance resources.
key_works: Grassie (2009), *Rail corrugation: Characteristics, causes, and treatments*, DOI:10.1243/09544097JRRT264.

title: Coordinated digital automatic coupling rollout
open: Develop financing, sequencing, and interoperability arrangements that make fleet conversion viable despite mixed-equipped trains and benefits shared among many actors.
status: Investment planning exists; network effects and transitional incompatibilities remain central deployment barriers.
why: Individually rational delayed adoption can prevent a beneficial network transition.
key_works: Europe’s Rail (2023), *European DAC Investment Plan*.

title: Route-specific replacement of diesel rail traction
open: Select and validate electrification, battery, or other low-emission traction portfolios using whole-route duty cycles, infrastructure, resilience, and lifecycle impacts.
status: Multiple technologies and demonstrations exist; no single option dominates every lightly used or remote route.
why: Avoids forcing an unsuitable decarbonization technology onto an entire railway.
key_works: Europe’s Rail, *RAIL4EARTH—A sustainable and green rail system*.

title: Truthful collaborative freight pooling
subfield: Freight, urban logistics, and cold chains
open: Allocate shared capacity and savings when carriers can misreport demand, costs, availability, or service quality.
status: Open logistics architectures motivate pooling; operational gains do not automatically produce incentive-compatible participation.
why: Collaboration fails when participants benefit from withholding or distorting information.
key_works: Montreuil (2011), *Toward a Physical Internet: Meeting the Global Logistics Sustainability Grand Challenge*, DOI:10.1007/s12159-011-0045-x.

title: Interoperable Physical Internet handling
subfield: Freight, urban logistics, and cold chains
open: Make modular freight units, handling equipment, identification, and routing interoperable across independent networks without excessive repacking or empty-unit circulation.
status: The Physical Internet supplies an architectural vision; universal operational compatibility is a larger engineering target.
why: Could enable freight to move through shared networks rather than isolated company systems.
key_works: Montreuil (2011), *Toward a Physical Internet*, DOI:10.1007/s12159-011-0045-x.

title: Real-world value of pooled human–robot logistics
subfield: Freight, urban logistics, and cold chains
open: Demonstrate that dynamic human–robot resource pooling reduces total delivery cost while preserving worker safety and service quality under real disruptions.
status: A 2026 study develops dynamic deployment models; sustained field performance is a separate validation target.
why: Simulated labor or robot utilization gains can disappear during execution.
key_works: Xu, Klibi, and Montreuil (2026), *Dynamic deployment of pooled human-robot resources in urban parcel logistics*, DOI:10.1016/j.trb.2026.103409.

title: Joint curb allocation and delivery routing
subfield: Freight, urban logistics, and cold chains
open: Optimize delivery routes jointly with time-varying legal stopping capacity, pedestrian access, congestion, and enforcement uncertainty.
status: City-logistics methods address routing and consolidation; the curb is often treated as available rather than a contested resource.
why: A route can be geographically short yet operationally infeasible.
key_works: Savelsbergh and Van Woensel (2016), *50th Anniversary Invited Article—City Logistics: Challenges and Opportunities*, DOI:10.1287/trsc.2016.0675.

title: Causal net benefit of urban microhubs
subfield: Freight, urban logistics, and cold chains
open: Measure whether a microhub reduces total vehicle travel and emissions after including replenishment, handling, empty trips, induced deliveries, and displaced curb activity.
status: Consolidation is a prominent city-logistics strategy; benefits depend on system boundaries and utilization.
why: A cleaner last kilometer can conceal a more expensive upstream operation.
key_works: Savelsbergh and Van Woensel (2016), *City Logistics: Challenges and Opportunities*.

title: Integrated forward and reverse urban logistics
subfield: Freight, urban logistics, and cold chains
open: Combine deliveries, returns, reusable packaging, and waste collection while handling uncertain timing, contamination constraints, and incompatible service requirements.
status: Reverse and omnichannel logistics have extensive models; robust integration across organizations remains a deployment target.
why: Empty return capacity is valuable only when operational constraints permit reuse.
key_works: Savelsbergh and Van Woensel (2016), *City Logistics: Challenges and Opportunities*.

title: Where additional truck parking actually helps
subfield: Freight, urban logistics, and cold chains
open: Estimate the causal safety and productivity benefit of adding parking at specific places and times, separately from improving information about existing spaces.
status: FMCSA’s 2025 research program explicitly targets quantification of parking benefits; aggregate space counts are insufficient.
why: Guides scarce land and funding toward consequential shortages.
key_works: FMCSA (2025), *Quantifying the Benefits of Truck Parking*; ATRI (2025), *State-Level Public Truck Parking Findings*.

title: Affordable off-grid cold-chain continuity
subfield: Freight, urban logistics, and cold chains
open: Maintain required product temperatures through unreliable electricity, loading delays, and transport disruptions at costs viable for small producers.
status: Sustainable cold-chain technologies exist; continuity, financing, and utilization remain jointly limiting.
why: Prevents food losses without creating unaffordable or emissions-intensive infrastructure.
key_works: UNEP and FAO (2022), *Sustainable food cold chains: Opportunities, challenges and the way forward*, DOI:10.4060/cc0923en.

title: Temperature-history-to-quality prediction
subfield: Freight, urban logistics, and cold chains
open: Predict remaining usable quality from complete, imperfect temperature histories across products, packaging, and microbial conditions.
status: Temperature monitoring is available; reliable quality inference is more demanding than detecting a threshold violation.
why: Enables rational routing and disposal decisions rather than blanket rejection.
key_works: UNEP and FAO (2022), *Sustainable food cold chains*, DOI:10.4060/cc0923en.

title: Joint food-loss and refrigeration-emissions optimization
subfield: Freight, urban logistics, and cold chains
open: Determine refrigeration, routing, and storage policies minimizing combined food-loss, energy, refrigerant, and equipment impacts.
status: Cold-chain sustainability work identifies interacting burdens; minimizing refrigeration energy alone can increase total harm.
why: Connects transport emissions with the larger footprint of spoiled products.
key_works: UNEP and FAO (2022), *Sustainable food cold chains*, DOI:10.4060/cc0923en.

title: Ammonia propulsion with low net climate impact
subfield: Marine propulsion, fuels, and ship environmental performance
open: Validate whole-voyage greenhouse performance of ammonia propulsion, including upstream production, nitrous oxide, pilot fuel, and transient operating conditions.
status: Engines and safety work have advanced; IMO’s September 2026 seminar still addresses substantial implementation questions.
why: Carbon-free fuel molecules do not guarantee low climate impact.
key_works: IMO (2026), *Technical Seminar on the use of ammonia as marine fuel*.

title: Ammonia bunkering risk under realistic failures
subfield: Marine propulsion, fuels, and ship environmental performance
open: Demonstrate effective detection, containment, evacuation, and response for credible toxic releases during bunkering and onboard handling.
status: Guidance and technical development exist; site-specific integrated safety performance remains necessary.
why: Toxicity creates risks different from conventional marine fuels.
key_works: IMO (2026), *Technical Seminar on the use of ammonia as marine fuel*.

title: Transient ammonia-engine emissions maps
subfield: Marine propulsion, fuels, and ship environmental performance
open: Measure and model ammonia slip, nitrogen oxides, and nitrous oxide during starts, load changes, low-load operation, and after-treatment degradation.
status: Steady operating points are insufficient for voyage-level assessment; transient emissions remain a key validation need.
why: Rare operating states may dominate important emissions.
key_works: IMO (2026), *Technical Seminar on the use of ammonia as marine fuel*.

title: Representative real-world methane slip
subfield: Marine propulsion, fuels, and ship environmental performance
open: Build representative methane-emission factors for ship engines across age, maintenance, load, weather, and voyage type.
status: FUMES combined airborne and onboard measurements; representative fleet coverage remains a larger data requirement.
why: Climate comparisons are sensitive to operating conditions omitted from certification tests.
key_works: ICCT (2024), *Fugitive and Unburned Methane Emissions from Ships—FUMES*.

title: Durable low-load methane abatement
subfield: Marine propulsion, fuels, and ship environmental performance
open: Reduce methane emissions during low-load and transient operation without unacceptable fuel penalties, maintenance burden, or loss of effectiveness over time.
status: Real-world measurements identify the importance of operating conditions; durable whole-duty-cycle abatement remains the engineering target.
why: Laboratory removal efficiency is insufficient for climate-effective service.
key_works: ICCT (2024), *Fugitive and Unburned Methane Emissions from Ships—FUMES*.

title: Reconciling ship methane measurements
subfield: Marine propulsion, fuels, and ship environmental performance
open: Reconcile engine measurements, ship-level observations, remote plume measurements, and fleet inventories within a common uncertainty framework.
status: Multiple measurement methods have been deployed; differing boundaries and sampling create reconciliation challenges.
why: Prevents incompatible inventories from supporting contradictory fuel policies.
key_works: ICCT (2024), *Fugitive and Unburned Methane Emissions from Ships—FUMES*.

title: Quiet propulsion without efficiency sacrifice
subfield: Marine propulsion, fuels, and ship environmental performance
open: Identify hull, propeller, and operating changes that reduce underwater radiated noise across service conditions while maintaining or improving energy efficiency.
status: IMO and MARAD are actively examining efficiency–noise interactions; co-benefits are not universal.
why: Avoids solving one environmental problem by worsening another.
key_works: MARAD (2025), *Vessel Generated Underwater Noise*; IMO (2025), *Workshop on the relationship between ship energy efficiency and underwater radiated noise*.

title: Ecologically meaningful ship-noise limits
subfield: Marine propulsion, fuels, and ship environmental performance
open: Connect cumulative, frequency-dependent vessel noise exposure to biological effects across species, habitats, and behavioral contexts.
status: Noise-reduction guidelines exist; translating acoustic measures into ecosystem outcomes remains an important evidence gap.
why: Decibel reductions alone do not establish ecological benefit.
key_works: IMO, *Ship noise*, including revised 2023 guidelines and subsequent implementation work.

title: In-water cleaning without biological release
subfield: Marine propulsion, fuels, and ship environmental performance
open: Remove biofouling while reliably capturing organisms and debris, avoiding invasive-species transfer and excessive coating damage.
status: IMO issued in-water cleaning guidance in 2025; validated performance across conditions remains a deployment requirement.
why: Hull cleaning can reduce fuel use while creating a different environmental pathway.
key_works: IMO (2025), *Guidance on in-water cleaning of ships’ biofouling*, MEPC.1/Circ.918.

title: Predictive biofouling maintenance
subfield: Marine propulsion, fuels, and ship environmental performance
open: Predict fouling growth and select cleaning or coating interventions using voyage history, idle periods, habitat, fuel penalty, and biological-transfer risk.
status: Guidelines and management practices exist; individualized lifecycle prediction remains the stronger target.
why: Fixed cleaning schedules miss substantial differences between vessels.
key_works: IMO (2023), *Guidelines for the control and management of ships’ biofouling*; IMO’s biofouling program.

title: Truthful just-in-time ship arrivals
subfield: Ports, inland waterways, and maritime networks
open: Make berth availability, completion times, and readiness information sufficiently reliable that ships can slow down without being penalized for arriving later.
status: Just-in-time arrival guidance identifies information and incentive barriers; technical ETA prediction alone is insufficient.
why: Removes wasteful “sail fast, then wait” behavior.
key_works: GEF–UNDP–IMO GloMEEP and GIA (2020), *Just In Time Arrival Guide—Barriers and Potential Solutions*.

title: Robust arrival control under changing berth readiness
subfield: Ports, inland waterways, and maritime networks
open: Continuously revise speed and arrival decisions as weather, congestion, and berth completion forecasts change, with bounded service and fuel penalties.
status: Just-in-time concepts and contracts exist; uncertainty-aware operational coordination remains necessary.
why: A single early ETA agreement cannot absorb an entire voyage’s uncertainty.
key_works: GloMEEP and GIA (2020), *Just In Time Arrival Guide*; BIMCO (2021), *Just in Time Arrival Clause for Voyage Charter Parties*.

title: Contractual sharing of arrival-efficiency gains
subfield: Ports, inland waterways, and maritime networks
open: Design enforceable arrangements that distribute fuel savings, delay risk, and opportunity costs among shipowners, charterers, terminals, and cargo owners.
status: BIMCO provides a contractual mechanism; universal alignment across commercial arrangements is not thereby established.
why: The actor paying for a change may not receive its benefits.
key_works: BIMCO (2021), *Just in Time Arrival Clause for Voyage Charter Parties 2021*.

title: Port electrification without grid bottleneck migration
subfield: Ports, inland waterways, and maritime networks
open: Coordinate shore power, cargo-handling equipment, truck charging, and grid upgrades under uncertain vessel calls and freight demand.
status: Port decarbonization is advancing, but shared electricity infrastructure creates new coupled constraints.
why: Electrifying separate assets can create coincident peaks that undermine the whole port.
key_works: UNCTAD (2025), *Review of Maritime Transport 2025: Staying the course in turbulent waters*.

title: Port asset condition linked to operational consequence
subfield: Ports, inland waterways, and maritime networks
open: Develop comparable condition and failure-risk data for quay walls, cranes, pavements, channels, and utilities, linked to cargo disruption.
status: Operational performance measures exist; translating heterogeneous asset condition into service risk remains a data-integration target.
why: Asset age alone poorly identifies the investments that prevent disruption.
key_works: UNCTAD (2025), *Review of Maritime Transport 2025*; Bierwirth and Meisel (2015), *A follow-up survey of berth allocation and quay crane scheduling problems in container terminals*.

title: Real-time integrated terminal recovery
subfield: Ports, inland waterways, and maritime networks
open: Recover berth, crane, yard, and vehicle schedules jointly after equipment failures or late vessels, with verifiable solution quality within operational deadlines.
status: Integrated optimizers and robust formulations exist; large-scale real-time recovery remains a stronger system target.
why: Optimizing one terminal subsystem can move congestion into another.
key_works: Bierwirth and Meisel (2015), *A follow-up survey of berth allocation and quay crane scheduling problems in container terminals*, DOI:10.1016/j.ejor.2014.12.030.

title: Drought-aware lock scheduling
subfield: Ports, inland waterways, and maritime networks
open: Jointly schedule vessels and lockages while accounting for water consumption, changing available depth, vessel heterogeneity, and time-sensitive cargo.
status: Waterway traffic models are developing; hydrological constraints make direct transplantation of road-traffic methods inadequate.
why: Throughput optimization can consume water needed for later operations.
key_works: Zhuang et al. (2024), *Traffic Flow Theory for Waterway Traffic: Current Challenges and Countermeasures*, DOI:10.3390/jmse12122254.

title: Fundamental diagrams for heterogeneous waterways
subfield: Ports, inland waterways, and maritime networks
open: Establish when meaningful flow–density relationships exist for vessels with different sizes, maneuverability, drafts, and navigation rules.
status: A 2024 review identifies difficulties adapting traffic-flow theory to waterways.
why: Channel capacity cannot safely be inferred from road analogies alone.
key_works: Zhuang, Liu, Wang, Guo, and Ni (2024), *Traffic Flow Theory for Waterway Traffic*, DOI:10.3390/jmse12122254.

title: Waterway intersection service and safety
subfield: Ports, inland waterways, and maritime networks
open: Derive capacity and delay measures that remain predictive when crossing, overtaking, restricted maneuverability, and collision-avoidance decisions interact.
status: Waterway-specific level-of-service methods exist; validated generalization across intersection types remains a target.
why: Average traffic volume can conceal dangerous conflict patterns.
key_works: Liu et al. (2024), *Level of Service Evaluation Method for Waterway Intersections*, DOI:10.3390/jmse12112050.

title: Resilient small-island shipping services
subfield: Ports, inland waterways, and maritime networks
open: Design fleet, subsidy, reserve-capacity, and fuel strategies that preserve affordable service under low demand and major route disruptions.
status: Maritime assessments document vulnerability and uneven transport costs; durable small-market solutions remain difficult.
why: Shipping disruption can threaten essential supplies rather than merely raise logistics costs.
key_works: UNCTAD (2025), *Review of Maritime Transport 2025: Staying the course in turbulent waters*.

title: Certifiable megawatt-class hybrid-electric propulsion
open: Demonstrate fault-tolerant, maintainable aircraft-wide hybrid-electric propulsion whose lifecycle benefits survive certification and operational requirements.
status: NASA reported hybrid-electric flight demonstration progress in 2026; first demonstration is not equivalent to fleet-ready integration.
why: Moves electrification from isolated components toward useful transport aircraft.
key_works: NASA (2026), *Electrified Powertrain Flight Demonstration* program and results.

title: Lightweight high-voltage insulation at altitude
open: Control partial discharge, arcing, contamination, and aging in high-voltage aircraft systems without insulation and protection mass erasing propulsion benefits.
status: Altitude testing has advanced; full-life behavior under combined environmental stresses remains an engineering requirement.
why: Ground-level electrical performance does not establish safe high-altitude operation.
key_works: NASA, *Electrified Powertrain Flight Demonstration*; NASA–magniX altitude-test reporting.

title: Aircraft-wide thermal management for electrification
open: Reject heat from motors, electronics, and storage across the flight envelope without unacceptable drag, mass, or failure coupling.
status: Electrified powertrain demonstrations address components and integration; aircraft-level thermal trade-offs remain mission-dependent.
why: Electrical efficiency improvements can be outweighed by cooling-system penalties.
key_works: Wen et al. (2023), *Fleet Wide Impacts of the Electrified Powertrain Flight Demonstration Technology Portfolio*, DOI:10.2514/6.2023-3871.

title: Net flight benefit of boundary-layer ingestion
open: Demonstrate net mission energy savings after accounting for distorted inflow, installation effects, structural changes, control, and off-design operation.
status: Modeling and coupled optimization have advanced; isolated propulsor or idealized benefits do not settle integrated flight performance.
why: Could recover energy otherwise lost in the aircraft wake.
key_works: Hendricks et al. (2018), *A Review of Boundary Layer Ingestion Modeling Approaches for Use in Conceptual Design*, NASA NTRS 20180005165.

title: Distortion-tolerant boundary-layer-ingesting propulsion
open: Maintain efficiency, operability, and acceptable fatigue under strongly nonuniform inflow across maneuvers and atmospheric disturbances.
status: BLI mechanisms and design approaches are actively studied; robust off-design operation remains a major integration requirement.
why: Wake-energy recovery is unusable if it creates unacceptable fan instability or fatigue.
key_works: Hall (2024), *Mechanisms, Benefits, and Challenges of Boundary Layer Ingestion Propulsion*; NASA (2025), *Advancements in Coupled Aeropropulsive Design Optimization*.

title: Lightweight hydrogen tanks with aircraft service life
open: Develop cryogenic storage that meets aircraft mass, fatigue, crashworthiness, insulation, inspection, and turnaround requirements simultaneously.
status: FlyZero developed aircraft concepts and technology roadmaps; satisfying the combined operational envelope remains the target.
why: Hydrogen’s mass advantage is constrained by storage volume and tank-system burden.
key_works: Aerospace Technology Institute (2022), *FlyZero: Our Vision for Zero-Carbon Emission Air Travel* and *Advanced Manufacturing*.

title: Rapid and safe hydrogen-aircraft turnaround
open: Demonstrate refueling, venting, leak detection, ground handling, and emergency procedures at service-relevant turnaround times.
status: Hydrogen aircraft concepts require airport integration beyond airborne propulsion feasibility.
why: An aircraft that cannot be turned around safely and economically is not a viable transport system.
key_works: Aerospace Technology Institute (2022), *FlyZero* technology and commercial roadmaps.

title: Whole-climate comparison of alternative aircraft energy
open: Compare batteries, hydrogen, and synthetic fuels using consistent mission, infrastructure, upstream-energy, and non-CO₂ climate boundaries.
status: Fundamentals-based energy comparisons exist; results depend strongly on assumptions and operational context.
why: Tailpipe carbon accounting alone can rank technologies incorrectly.
key_works: Aerospace Technology Institute (2022), *Primary Energy Source Comparison and Selection*, FlyZero.

title: Supercooled-large-droplet icing prediction
open: Validate models of large-droplet impingement, splashing, runback, and freezing outside conventional protected regions.
status: NASA’s October 5, 2026 report describes new tunnel instrumentation and continuing analysis specifically addressing this gap.
why: Existing icing protection can miss where large droplets deposit water.
key_works: Mann/NASA (2026), *NASA Testing Aims at Supercooled Large Droplet Aviation Safety*.

title: Community response to repeated low-boom flight
open: Determine acceptable exposure to repeated shaped sonic booms across buildings, activities, populations, and atmospheric conditions.
status: X-59 flight testing has advanced in 2026; flight capability alone does not establish community acceptability.
why: Low-boom transport requires social and acoustic evidence beyond a single overflight.
key_works: NASA (2026), *NASA’s X-59 Aircraft Flies Supersonic for First Time* and continuing Quesst flight-test reporting.

title: Humidity forecasts for contrail decisions
subfield: Air traffic, contrails, drones, and advanced air mobility
open: Predict ice-supersaturated regions accurately enough that rerouting decisions remain beneficial after forecast uncertainty is included.
status: Contrail-energy predictions are sensitive to humidity and model parameters; uncertainty-aware prediction remains central.
why: Incorrect avoidance forecasts waste fuel without preventing warming.
key_works: Platt et al. (2024), *The effect of uncertainty in humidity and model parameters on the prediction of contrail energy forcing*.

title: Satellite detection bias in contrail evaluation
subfield: Air traffic, contrails, drones, and advanced air mobility
open: Quantify contrails missed or misclassified by satellite observations and correct evaluation metrics for those selection effects.
status: A 2025 study identifies factors limiting detection; observed contrails are not a complete census.
why: Avoidance trials can appear successful merely because their outcomes become harder to observe.
key_works: Driver et al. (2025), *Factors limiting contrail detection in satellite imagery*, DOI:10.5194/amt-18-1115-2025.

title: Causal climate benefit of contrail avoidance
subfield: Air traffic, contrails, drones, and advanced air mobility
open: Measure the causal change in climate forcing from operational avoidance, rather than relying solely on modeled contrail occurrence or estimated energy forcing.
status: A 2026 Asia-Pacific trial reported promising estimated effects; modeled impact is not direct measurement of realized forcing.
why: Establishes whether operational changes deliver the intended climate benefit.
key_works: Armada and Vogler (2026), *Our new contrail avoidance trial in Asia-Pacific*; Bräuer et al. (2021), DOI:10.1029/2020GL092166.

title: Joint fuel–contrail dispatch optimization
subfield: Air traffic, contrails, drones, and advanced air mobility
open: Choose avoidance actions robustly when extra fuel emissions, contrail forcing, airspace constraints, and forecast errors interact.
status: Avoidance trials and uncertainty studies provide components; dependable whole-network optimization remains the stronger target.
why: Preventing one contrail can increase another flight’s fuel use or delay.
key_works: Platt et al. (2024), *The effect of uncertainty…*; Armada and Vogler (2026), *Our new contrail avoidance trial in Asia-Pacific*.

title: Multi-operator low-altitude deconfliction
subfield: Air traffic, contrails, drones, and advanced air mobility
open: Coordinate independent fleets with incomplete information while guaranteeing separation and recovering safely from inconsistent plans or failed services.
status: NASA’s High Density Vertiplex work integrates prototype systems and multivehicle tests; broad interoperable operation remains a larger requirement.
why: Each operator’s safe plan can conflict with another operator’s plan.
key_works: Schaefer et al. (2024), *High Density Vertiplex—Scalable Autonomous Operations—Flight Test Report*, NASA NTRS 20240007438.

title: Missed approaches in dense vertiport networks
subfield: Air traffic, contrails, drones, and advanced air mobility
open: Develop procedures that preserve safe escape and diversion options when several arrivals miss approaches during correlated weather or infrastructure failures.
status: NASA has explored missed-approach concepts; dense interacting operations require broader validation.
why: Nominal arrival capacity is misleading without protected recovery capacity.
key_works: NASA (2023), *Missed Approach Procedures in Advanced Air Mobility: Conceptual Exploration*, NTRS 20230007215.

title: Human supervision limits for aircraft fleets
subfield: Air traffic, contrails, drones, and advanced air mobility
open: Determine safe supervision ratios as a function of automation reliability, alert correlation, task complexity, and operator fatigue.
status: Human–autonomy teaming research identifies the challenge; a fixed vehicles-per-operator number cannot cover all conditions.
why: Labor savings depend on avoiding overload during exceptional events.
key_works: Holbrook et al. (2020), *Enabling Urban Air Mobility: Human-Autonomy Teaming Research Challenges and Recommendations*, NTRS 20205002387.

title: Safe handover during simultaneous aircraft emergencies
subfield: Air traffic, contrails, drones, and advanced air mobility
open: Allocate attention and authority when multiple aircraft require intervention at once, with explicit guarantees on unattended vehicles.
status: Human–autonomy research recognizes teaming and responsibility issues; correlated emergencies are a stronger stress case than isolated alerts.
why: Rare common-cause events can defeat otherwise efficient fleet supervision.
key_works: Holbrook et al. (2020), *Enabling Urban Air Mobility: Human-Autonomy Teaming Research Challenges and Recommendations*.

title: Vertiport slots coupled to charging and reserves
subfield: Air traffic, contrails, drones, and advanced air mobility
open: Schedule arrivals, departures, charging, passenger handling, and diversion reserves jointly under uncertain energy and turnaround times.
status: Integrated vertiport prototypes exist; small-aircraft surrogate tests do not close every full-scale capacity constraint.
why: A landing pad can be available while the aircraft’s onward operation is infeasible.
key_works: Schaefer et al. (2024), *High Density Vertiplex—Scalable Autonomous Operations—Flight Test Report*.

title: Fleet-interface usability under operational stress
subfield: Air traffic, contrails, drones, and advanced air mobility
open: Validate whether interfaces remain usable during long shifts, unfamiliar failures, high alert rates, and diverse operator experience.
status: NASA has evaluated fleet-management interfaces; laboratory usability does not establish resilient operational performance.
why: Automation can shift rather than remove workload.
key_works: NASA (2022), *Usability Evaluation of Fleet Management Interface for High Density Vertiplex Environments*, NTRS 20220009874.

title: Explaining divergent road-fatality trends
open: Separate exposure, speed, vehicle mix, infrastructure, behavior, reporting, and emergency-care contributions to changing fatality rates across populations.
status: Global monitoring documents large differences; aggregate trends do not identify the best causal intervention.
why: Different causes require different countermeasures.
key_works: WHO (2023), *Global status report on road safety 2023*.

title: Comparable serious-injury surveillance
open: Link police, hospital, emergency-service, and mortality records to estimate serious injuries consistently while correcting underreporting.
status: Fatalities receive more consistent attention than nonfatal outcomes; comparable injury surveillance remains an important gap.
why: Fatality-only metrics miss a large burden of lifelong disability.
key_works: WHO (2023), *Global status report on road safety 2023*.

title: Cost-effective post-crash care expansion
open: Identify which combinations of dispatch, first response, transport, and trauma capability most reduce preventable death in underserved regions.
status: Post-crash response is part of established road-safety strategy; locally transferable allocation evidence remains necessary.
why: Similar crashes can have very different outcomes depending on access to care.
key_works: WHO (2023), *Global status report on road safety 2023*.

title: Network effects of crossing retrofits
open: Measure whether a crossing improvement reduces total injury risk after pedestrians and drivers reroute, rather than evaluating the treated crossing alone.
status: Individual countermeasures have evidence; network spillovers and route substitution require additional evaluation.
why: Local safety gains may be offset or amplified elsewhere.
key_works: FHWA, *Pedestrian Hybrid Beacons*, Proven Safety Countermeasures.

title: Safety retrofit portfolios under fixed budgets
open: Select combinations of proven treatments that maximize serious-injury reduction while accounting for uncertainty, interactions, and distributional constraints.
status: Treatment evidence does not uniquely determine the best network-wide portfolio.
why: Budget allocation matters as much as identifying effective individual devices.
key_works: FHWA, *Proven Safety Countermeasures*, including *Pedestrian Hybrid Beacons*.

title: Causal sources of unequal road trauma
open: Quantify how infrastructure, exposure, vehicle access, enforcement, and care contribute to disproportionate injury burdens without attributing structural differences to individual behavior alone.
status: Transportation inequities are documented; explanatory and intervention-ready metrics remain incomplete.
why: Enables interventions that address causes rather than merely describing disparities.
key_works: National Academies (2024), *Critical Issues in Transportation for 2024 and Beyond*, “Promoting Equity and Inclusion.”

title: Long-term adaptation to driver assistance
open: Measure how sustained assistance changes attention, skill, trust, and risk-taking, and determine whether initial safety benefits persist.
status: Transition experiments establish substantial human variability; longitudinal adaptation requires longer observation than one-session studies.
why: Drivers can adapt to automation in ways that alter its eventual effect.
key_works: Eriksson and Stanton (2017), *Takeover Time in Highly Automated Vehicles: Noncritical Transitions to and From Manual Control*, DOI:10.1177/0018720816685832.

title: Tail-safe takeover timing
open: Design takeover policies for the slow and unreliable tails of human response, accounting for task engagement, impairment, and situation complexity.
status: Experimental takeover times vary widely; designing around a mean or median is inadequate.
why: Safety-critical transitions are determined by tail behavior.
key_works: Eriksson and Stanton (2017), *Takeover Time in Highly Automated Vehicles*, DOI:10.1177/0018720816685832.

title: Pedestrian-safe large-vehicle geometry
open: Identify feasible front-end designs that reduce pedestrian harm across stature and impact speed while satisfying visibility, cooling, crashworthiness, and utility requirements.
status: Real-world studies associate taller, blunter fronts with greater fatality risk; integrated redesign remains the engineering target.
why: Avoidance technology cannot prevent every collision.
key_works: IIHS (2023), *Vehicles with higher, more vertical front ends pose greater risk to pedestrians*.

title: Representative pedestrian-impact evaluation
open: Develop test populations and injury models covering children, older adults, different body sizes, and mobility-device users rather than relying on a narrow surrogate.
