status: Geometry–fatality associations motivate broader evaluation; population coverage remains a distinct evidence requirement.
why: A design optimized for one test body may protect others poorly.
key_works: IIHS (2023), *Vehicles with higher, more vertical front ends pose greater risk to pedestrians*.

title: Statistically defensible rare-event safety assurance
open: Combine simulation, targeted testing, operational data, and formal arguments into calibrated estimates of rare severe failures.
status: Conventional mileage accumulation can require impractically large exposure; alternative evidence must avoid unvalidated extrapolation.
why: Makes safety claims testable without waiting for enormous numbers of crashes.
key_works: Kalra and Paddock (2016), *Driving to Safety: How Many Miles of Driving Would It Take to Demonstrate Autonomous Vehicle Reliability?*, RAND RR-1478.

title: Simulation-to-road risk calibration
open: Quantify how simulator errors change estimated collision risk and establish when simulated improvements predict real operational improvements.
status: Open driving simulators enable extensive testing; visual realism does not establish risk fidelity.
why: A controller can exploit simulator weaknesses without becoming safer.
key_works: Dosovitskiy et al. (2017), *CARLA: An Open Urban Driving Simulator*, arXiv:1711.03938.

title: Closed-loop planning metrics aligned with safety
open: Determine which benchmark metrics predict safe, efficient closed-loop behavior rather than similarity to a recorded human trajectory.
status: nuPlan supplies closed-loop evaluation; deciding which metrics are causally meaningful remains a further problem.
why: A plausible trajectory prediction is not necessarily a competent driving policy.
key_works: Caesar et al. (2021), *nuPlan: A closed-loop ML-based planning benchmark for autonomous vehicles*, arXiv:2106.11810.

title: Counterfactual realism of simulated road users
open: Model how other drivers and pedestrians respond when an autonomous vehicle takes actions unlike those in recorded data.
status: Data-driven interactive simulators have advanced; counterfactual behavior is only partially constrained by logged trajectories.
why: Replay-based testing cannot reveal every interactive failure.
key_works: Gulino et al. (2023), *Waymax: An Accelerated, Data-Driven Simulator for Large-Scale Autonomous Driving Research*, arXiv:2310.08710.

title: Formal safety with uncertain perception
open: Connect perception uncertainty to formal driving guarantees without assuming perfectly known object states or unreasonably conservative behavior.
status: Formal driving models specify safety rules under assumptions; integrating calibrated perception uncertainty is a broader challenge.
why: A correct planner cannot compensate for an unrecognized hazard unless uncertainty is represented.
key_works: Shalev-Shwartz, Shammah, and Shashua (2017), *On a Formal Model of Safe and Scalable Self-driving Cars*, arXiv:1708.06374.

title: Safe driving without interaction deadlock
open: Guarantee useful progress in ambiguous negotiations without sacrificing safety or assuming other users always cooperate.
status: Formal safety frameworks address collision responsibility; liveness under uncertain social interaction remains a separate requirement.
why: A vehicle that never crashes because it never proceeds is not useful transportation.
key_works: Shalev-Shwartz, Shammah, and Shashua (2017), *On a Formal Model of Safe and Scalable Self-driving Cars*.

title: Sensor fusion under asymmetric weather degradation
open: Maintain calibrated object detection when fog, rain, spray, glare, or contamination degrades sensors differently and in previously unseen combinations.
status: Adverse-weather datasets and adaptive fusion improve robustness; coverage of rare combinations remains incomplete.
why: Sensor redundancy fails when confidence does not track changing sensor reliability.
key_works: Bijelic et al. (2020), *Seeing Through Fog Without Seeing Fog: Deep Multimodal Sensor Fusion in Unseen Adverse Weather*, arXiv:1902.08913.

title: Ground truth for extreme-weather driving
open: Obtain trustworthy object, visibility, friction, and sensor-state labels when ordinary labeling sensors are themselves degraded.
status: Large adverse-weather datasets exist, but severe conditions are rare and difficult to annotate reliably.
why: A benchmark cannot validate robustness when its reference labels are unreliable.
key_works: Bijelic et al. (2020), *Seeing Through Fog Without Seeing Fog*, arXiv:1902.08913.

title: Reliable operational-domain boundary detection
open: Detect departure from a validated operating domain early enough to reach a safe state, including gradual and interacting changes.
status: Defined operating domains and test environments exist; reliable online recognition of their boundaries is a stronger operational requirement.
why: Safety evidence is conditional on knowing when its assumptions apply.
key_works: Kalra and Paddock (2016), *Driving to Safety*; Dosovitskiy et al. (2017), *CARLA*.

title: Autonomous service recovery beyond nominal driving
open: Complete or safely resolve journeys after blocked pickup locations, inaccessible drop-offs, vehicle faults, or communication loss without relying on undocumented human rescue.
status: Driving benchmarks emphasize motion planning; end-to-end service recovery requires additional tasks and evidence.
why: Successful driving segments do not guarantee completed transportation.
key_works: Caesar et al. (2021), *nuPlan*; Gulino et al. (2023), *Waymax*.

title: Tenfold fewer failed public charging sessions
open: As a proposed moonshot, reduce failed charging sessions tenfold against a matched baseline, including payment, authentication, connection, power delivery, and completion.
status: A published field study found only 73.3% of 655 tested ports functional; reported uptime is not identical to successful charging.
why: Reliability directly affects practical vehicle usability.
key_works: Rempel et al. (2024), *Reliability of Open Public Electric Vehicle Direct Current Fast Chargers*, DOI:10.1177/00187208231215242.

title: Physically accessible charging across vehicle designs
open: Make charging usable across inlet locations, cable weights, vehicle dimensions, and user mobility limitations without requiring unsafe parking or assistance.
status: Field reliability work identifies physical usability failures as well as electronic faults.
why: An energized charger can still be unusable.
key_works: Rempel et al. (2024), *Reliability of Open Public Electric Vehicle Direct Current Fast Chargers*.

title: Megawatt charging without excessive grid delay
open: Deploy heavy-duty charging at freight-relevant locations while coordinating interconnection, storage, power sharing, and uncertain demand growth.
status: The 2024 National Zero-Emission Freight Corridor Strategy provides a phased framework; execution requires local power-system solutions.
why: Truck deployment can outpace usable charging infrastructure.
key_works: Joint Office and partner agencies (2024), *National Zero-Emission Freight Corridor Strategy*.

title: Heavy-duty charging schedules compatible with battery life
open: Jointly optimize charging rate, battery temperature, delivery schedule, payload, and degradation over real freight duty cycles.
status: Corridor planning and electrification studies establish the need; useful optimization must include long-term asset effects.
why: Fast charging can trade today’s productivity against tomorrow’s battery availability.
key_works: *National Zero-Emission Freight Corridor Strategy* (2024); ACEEE (2026), *Advancing Zero-Emission Freight Corridors*.

title: Financing initially underused freight charging
open: Structure staged investment and risk-sharing so essential corridors can open before high utilization, without locking in persistently uneconomic assets.
status: National strategies recognize phased deployment; the adoption–infrastructure coordination problem remains site-specific.
why: Waiting for demand and waiting for infrastructure can reinforce one another.
key_works: Joint Office and partner agencies (2024), *National Zero-Emission Freight Corridor Strategy*.

title: Interoperable vehicle-to-grid operation
open: Make bidirectional charging work across vehicle, charger, aggregator, utility, and regional grid-code combinations without proprietary pairing.
status: The IEA’s 2026 assessment describes commercial implementations alongside continuing interoperability and conformance work.
why: A large theoretical storage resource is useless if only selected combinations can participate.
key_works: IEA (2026), *Vehicle-to-grid technology*.

title: Battery-wear compensation for vehicle-to-grid
open: Estimate incremental degradation and allocate compensation, warranty responsibility, and operating limits transparently across participants.
status: The IEA identifies battery-life and business-model questions as important deployment issues.
why: Grid-service revenue is not profit if vehicle owners absorb hidden battery costs.
key_works: IEA (2026), *Vehicle-to-grid technology*.

title: Firm grid services from uncertain vehicle availability
open: Offer reliable aggregate power while vehicles arrive late, depart early, change travel plans, or decline participation.
status: Aggregation can provide services, but dependable commitments require explicit mobility uncertainty and user guarantees.
why: Transportation needs can override a grid dispatch instruction.
key_works: IEA (2026), *Vehicle-to-grid technology*.

title: Charging reliability across weather and aging
open: Measure and reduce session failures across heat, cold, precipitation, equipment age, and maintenance practices using longitudinal rather than one-time audits.
status: Field audits expose failures; full seasonal and lifecycle reliability is a broader evidence requirement.
why: A successful inspection does not establish year-round service.
key_works: Rempel et al. (2024), *Reliability of Open Public Electric Vehicle Direct Current Fast Chargers*.

title: Transport electrification with less critical-mineral dependence
open: Achieve required vehicle service using battery chemistry, vehicle design, utilization, and recycling strategies that materially reduce critical-mineral demand.
status: The 2024 National Academies agenda identifies technical and cost barriers to less mineral-dependent battery designs.
why: Decarbonization should not assume unconstrained materials supply.
key_works: National Academies (2024), *Critical Issues in Transportation for 2024 and Beyond*, research appendix.

title: Pavement lifecycle assessment with realistic use-phase feedback
open: Integrate construction, maintenance, roughness-related vehicle energy, traffic delay, and end-of-life impacts using uncertainty-aware local data.
status: Reference frameworks exist; results remain sensitive to boundaries, deterioration assumptions, and traffic conditions.
why: Low construction emissions do not necessarily imply low lifetime impact.
key_works: Van Dam et al. (2015), *Towards Sustainable Pavement Systems: A Reference Document*, FHWA-HIF-15-002.

title: Recycled asphalt with predictable long-term durability
open: Predict performance across heterogeneous reclaimed materials, rejuvenators, climates, and loading without relying on short-term laboratory proxies alone.
status: Recycling strategies are established; reliable transfer from material tests to long service lives remains challenging.
why: Premature replacement can cancel material and emissions savings.
key_works: FHWA (2016), *Strategies for Improving the Sustainability of Asphalt Pavements*, FHWA-HIF-16-012.

title: Pavement design for nonstationary climate
open: Translate changing heat, rainfall, freeze–thaw, and flooding into design and rehabilitation decisions with quantified failure probabilities.
status: Climate-adaptation guidance exists; historical climate assumptions are insufficient for future service conditions.
why: Infrastructure may outlive the climate regime used to design it.
key_works: FHWA (2015), *Climate Change Adaptation for Pavements*; FHWA pavement sustainability resources.

title: Bridge condition to residual capacity
open: Infer load-bearing capacity and failure risk from inspection and sensing data, rather than treating visual condition ratings as direct measures of structural safety.
status: The Long-Term Bridge Performance program collects richer evidence; condition forecasting remains an active research product.
why: Similar visible damage can imply different structural consequences.
key_works: FHWA, *Long-Term Bridge Performance Program* and *InfoBridge* condition-forecast research.

title: Tenfold cheaper decision-grade bridge inspection
open: As a proposed moonshot, reduce inspection cost per defensible maintenance decision tenfold while maintaining detection sensitivity and uncertainty calibration.
status: Standardized protocols and remote sensing provide foundations; cheaper data collection is not automatically cheaper reliable decision-making.
why: Enables more frequent assessment of large aging inventories.
key_works: Hooks and Weidner, *Long-Term Bridge Performance Program Protocols, Version 1*, FHWA-HRT-16-007.

title: Abutment scour in cohesive soils
open: Develop validated prediction methods for abutment scour in cohesive materials across realistic hydraulic histories and geotechnical conditions.
status: The 2026 review identifies comparatively limited abutment-scour information relative to pier scour.
why: Sand-based extrapolations can misrepresent cohesive erosion.
key_works: Sheefa, Liu, Vitton, and Barkdoll (2026), *A Review on Bridge Scour Analysis in Cohesive Soils and Scour-Susceptible Rocks*, DOI:10.3390/w18151879.

title: Contraction scour in erodible rock
open: Predict contraction-driven erosion where fractured or weathered rock does not behave like either intact bedrock or cohesionless sediment.
status: The 2026 review identifies contraction scour in cohesive and rock formations as comparatively underdeveloped.
why: Misclassified rock resistance can lead to unsafe foundation assumptions.
key_works: Sheefa et al. (2026), *A Review on Bridge Scour Analysis in Cohesive Soils and Scour-Susceptible Rocks*.

title: Undisturbed erodibility characterization
open: Obtain samples and measurements that preserve the in-situ structure controlling erosion, then quantify sampling-induced bias.
status: The 2026 scour review identifies undisturbed sampling and appropriate erodibility tests as critical unresolved practical needs.
why: A precise laboratory test can still characterize the wrong material state.
key_works: Sheefa et al. (2026), *A Review on Bridge Scour Analysis in Cohesive Soils and Scour-Susceptible Rocks*.

title: Landscape-scale prediction of bridge scour
open: Couple local scour calculations to channel migration, sediment supply, watershed change, and sequences of floods over a bridge’s service life.
status: Guidance and geomorphic research exist; local hydraulic calculations do not capture every long-term landscape process.
why: A foundation can become exposed through processes outside the immediate bridge opening.
key_works: NCHRP (2011), *Evaluation of Bridge Scour Research: Geomorphic Processes and Predictions*, Web-Only Document 177; USGS (2003), *Guidance for Bridge Scour Studies*.

title: Causal service-life benefit of bridge maintenance
open: Estimate how specific interventions alter deterioration and failure risk while correcting for the fact that the worst bridges receive treatment first.
status: Longitudinal bridge programs provide data; observational maintenance histories contain strong selection effects.
why: Better forecasts do not automatically identify better interventions.
key_works: FHWA, *Long-Term Bridge Performance* program and InfoBridge research models.

title: Comparable non-exhaust particulate inventories
open: Measure and reconcile tire, brake, road-wear, and resuspended particles across vehicle classes, operating conditions, and measurement methods.
status: Non-exhaust emissions are recognized as important; standardized attribution and comparable inventories remain difficult.
why: Electrification does not remove all traffic-related particulate pollution.
key_works: OECD (2020), *Non-exhaust Particulate Emissions from Road Transport: An Ignored Environmental Policy Challenge*, DOI:10.1787/4a4dc6ca-en.

title: Regenerative braking’s real particle effects
open: Quantify brake-particle reductions and changed particle characteristics across regenerative strategies, friction-brake use, corrosion, and emergency braking.
status: Regeneration changes brake use, but whole-duty-cycle emissions depend on more than total braking energy.
why: Fleet models need realistic benefits rather than fixed assumed reduction factors.
key_works: Costagliola et al. (2024), *Non-Exhaust Particulate Emissions from Road Transport Vehicles*, DOI:10.3390/en17164079.

title: Safer replacements for 6PPD
open: Identify tire-protection chemistries that preserve safety and durability without producing comparably harmful transformation products.
status: Acute toxicity of 6PPD-quinone to coho salmon is established; finding and validating safer functional replacements is a different problem.
why: Removing an environmental hazard must not compromise tire integrity.
key_works: Tian et al. (2021), *A ubiquitous tire rubber-derived chemical induces acute mortality in coho salmon*, DOI:10.1126/science.abd6951.

title: Fate and chronic effects of tire-derived toxicants
open: Determine transport, transformation, bioavailability, and chronic effects across watersheds and species beyond the initially identified acute endpoint.
status: Identification of one potent toxicant does not complete environmental fate or ecosystem-risk assessment.
why: Guides runoff treatment and material substitution toward relevant exposure pathways.
key_works: Tian et al. (2021), *A ubiquitous tire rubber-derived chemical induces acute mortality in coho salmon*.

title: Low-wear tires without safety or energy penalties
open: Improve the joint frontier of particle generation, wet grip, rolling resistance, durability, and cold-weather performance.
status: Non-exhaust mitigation is an active policy and engineering need; optimizing one property can degrade another.
why: Avoids emissions improvements that increase crashes or energy consumption.
key_works: OECD (2020), *Non-exhaust Particulate Emissions from Road Transport*; Costagliola et al. (2024), *Non-Exhaust Particulate Emissions from Road Transport Vehicles*.

title: Probabilistic transport design under climate uncertainty
open: Develop usable design standards that explicitly incorporate changing hazard distributions, model disagreement, and consequences of failure.
status: Resilience guidance is advancing; translating uncertainty into procurement-ready design requirements remains difficult.
why: Neither historical return periods nor a single climate scenario is sufficient.
key_works: Global Center on Adaptation (2025), *Climate-Resilient Infrastructure Officer Handbook*.

title: Cascading transport–power–water failures
open: Predict and reduce cascades in which transport disruption blocks utility repair while utility outages disable transport operations.
status: Infrastructure resilience research recognizes interdependence; actionable coupled models remain demanding.
why: Independent asset hardening can miss shared failure pathways.
key_works: Hallegatte, Rentschler, and Rozenberg (2019), *Lifelines: The Resilient Infrastructure Opportunity*; GFDRR resilient-infrastructure program.

title: Equitable restoration of transportation access
open: Prioritize repair and temporary service using essential-access loss and vulnerability, not only traffic volume or economic output.
status: Resilience frameworks emphasize service consequences; operational equity criteria remain difficult to specify and validate.
why: Low-volume links can be indispensable to isolated communities.
key_works: Hallegatte, Rentschler, and Rozenberg (2019), *Lifelines*; GFDRR, *Resilient Infrastructure*.

title: Avoiding transport adaptation that relocates risk
open: Evaluate whether raising, defending, rerouting, or expanding infrastructure increases flood exposure, displacement, or ecological damage elsewhere.
status: Climate-resilience guidance increasingly requires systemwide assessment; local asset protection is not sufficient evidence of net benefit.
why: A protected road can worsen flooding or access for neighboring communities.
key_works: Global Center on Adaptation (2025), *Climate-Resilient Infrastructure Officer Handbook*.

title: Operational adaptation to compound extremes
open: Maintain essential mobility during combinations such as heat plus power outage, wildfire plus evacuation, or flooding plus communications failure.
status: Transportation resilience conferences document these challenges; compound-event operations remain more complex than single-hazard plans.
why: Independently adequate contingency plans can fail when activated together.
key_works: National Academies (2025), *Transportation Resilience 2023: International Conference on Extreme Weather and Climate Change Challenges*, DOI:10.17226/28858.

title: Replacing fuel taxes without regressive surveillance
subfield: Institutions, financing, rural access, and informal transport
open: Develop durable road-revenue systems that protect privacy, address affordability, and remain administratively workable as vehicle energy sources change.
status: The National Academies identify replacement revenue and equity consequences as unresolved policy questions.
why: Infrastructure funding must not depend indefinitely on declining taxable fuel consumption.
key_works: National Academies (2024), *Critical Issues in Transportation for 2024 and Beyond*, “Funding and Finance.”

title: Binding maintenance funding commitments
subfield: Institutions, financing, rural access, and informal transport
open: Design funding and accountability arrangements that prevent predictable maintenance needs from being repeatedly deferred in favor of more visible projects.
status: Maintenance and financial sustainability remain recurring transport funding problems.
why: Deferred work can turn manageable deterioration into costly loss of service.
key_works: National Academies (2024), *Critical Issues in Transportation for 2024 and Beyond*, “Funding and Finance.”

title: Cross-jurisdiction corridor coordination
subfield: Institutions, financing, rural access, and informal transport
open: Allocate investment, operating responsibility, and benefits across jurisdictions whose local incentives conflict with corridor-wide performance.
status: Fragmented governance is an identified barrier; cooperation requires more than compatible engineering designs.
why: Bottlenecks and externalities routinely cross administrative boundaries.
key_works: National Academies (2024), *Critical Issues in Transportation for 2024 and Beyond*, “Governance.”

title: When private provision actually improves outcomes
subfield: Institutions, financing, rural access, and informal transport
open: Identify causal conditions under which private participation improves lifecycle cost, service, innovation, and risk allocation rather than merely changing accounting treatment.
status: Comparative governance remains context-dependent; ownership labels alone do not predict performance.
why: Poorly allocated risk can leave the public paying for nominally private projects.
key_works: National Academies (2024), *Critical Issues in Transportation for 2024 and Beyond*, “Governance.”

title: Retaining public-sector transport expertise
subfield: Institutions, financing, rural access, and informal transport
open: Test staffing, procurement, compensation, training, and career structures that retain the technical capacity needed to oversee increasingly complex systems.
status: The 2024 workforce agenda explicitly identifies attraction, training, and retention as unresolved needs.
why: Agencies cannot effectively buy or regulate systems they cannot evaluate.
key_works: National Academies (2024), *Critical Issues in Transportation for 2024 and Beyond*, “Workforce.”

title: Complementary investments that make rural roads productive
subfield: Institutions, financing, rural access, and informal transport
open: Identify which combinations of roads, services, finance, skills, and market institutions convert improved connectivity into sustained household gains.
status: Rural-road evidence shows labor reallocation without automatic broad income gains over the measured horizon.
why: Connectivity is an input to development, not a guarantee of it.
key_works: Asher and Novosad (2020), *Rural Roads and Local Economic Development*, DOI:10.1257/aer.20180268.

title: Rural access beyond proximity to a road
subfield: Institutions, financing, rural access, and informal transport
open: Measure whether people can afford and obtain reliable transport to essential destinations, not merely whether an all-season road is nearby.
status: Rural Access Index methods improve physical-connectivity measurement; service availability and affordability require additional indicators.
why: A nearby road without usable transport does not provide effective access.
key_works: World Bank (2016), *Measuring Rural Access: Using New Technologies*.

title: Dynamic seasonal passability maps
subfield: Institutions, financing, rural access, and informal transport
open: Maintain route-level passability information through rain, flooding, erosion, and seasonal closures where fixed road inventories become misleading.
status: Geospatial rural-access methods exist; continually updated operational accessibility remains a larger data challenge.
why: Annual average access can conceal months of isolation.
key_works: World Bank (2019), *Measuring Rural Access: Update 2017/18*; Rural Access Index data program.

title: Maintained maps of informal transit
subfield: Institutions, financing, rural access, and informal transport
open: Keep routes, stops, fares, operating periods, and service changes current without requiring formal schedules or centralized operator records.
status: Digital Matatus demonstrated practical mapping and standardized data; long-term maintenance and scaling remain distinct challenges.
why: One-time maps quickly lose value in adaptive transport systems.
key_works: Digital Matatus project; MIT Department of Urban Studies and Planning, *Digital Matatus*.

title: Routing through unscheduled informal services
subfield: Institutions, financing, rural access, and informal transport
open: Provide useful multimodal journey predictions when departures, routes, fares, and transfer opportunities are uncertain or negotiated.
status: Mapping informal networks is feasible; dependable journey planning needs uncertainty models beyond static route geometry.
why: Treating informal transit as either perfectly scheduled or nonexistent both misrepresent mobility.
key_works: Digital Matatus research and data program.

title: Useful mobility data without reidentification
subfield: Transportation data, cybersecurity, and benchmark infrastructure
open: Release or analyze detailed movement data while bounding reidentification risk under realistic auxiliary information.
status: Mobility traces have long been shown to be highly identifying; removing names is not adequate protection.
why: Transportation research needs detail that is inherently sensitive.
key_works: de Montjoye, Hidalgo, Verleysen, and Blondel (2013), *Unique in the Crowd: The privacy bounds of human mobility*, DOI:10.1038/srep01376.

title: Privacy for rare origin–destination movements
subfield: Transportation data, cybersecurity, and benchmark infrastructure
open: Preserve useful estimates for rare trips and underserved groups while providing meaningful privacy protection over repeated data releases.
status: High mobility uniqueness creates a difficult utility–privacy trade-off, especially for sparse movements.
why: Privacy protection that deletes rare travel can erase the people most in need of service.
key_works: de Montjoye et al. (2013), *Unique in the Crowd*, DOI:10.1038/srep01376.

title: Safe vehicles connected to compromised chargers
subfield: Transportation data, cybersecurity, and benchmark infrastructure
open: Ensure that a malicious or compromised charger cannot induce unsafe vehicle behavior or propagate access into safety-critical systems.
status: NHTSA identifies compromised charging infrastructure and zero-trust vehicle architectures as active research concerns.
why: Charging expands the boundary between vehicles and externally controlled systems.
key_works: NHTSA (2024), *NHTSA/SAE Cybersecurity Workshop Keynote* and associated research agenda.

title: Safe over-the-air update and rollback
subfield: Transportation data, cybersecurity, and benchmark infrastructure
open: Verify that interrupted, inconsistent, or rolled-back updates cannot create unsafe combinations of vehicle software and calibration.
status: NHTSA’s 2022 practices address cybersecurity and software assurance; fleet-wide compositional correctness remains an engineering target.
why: Individually valid components can form an invalid vehicle configuration.
key_works: NHTSA (2022), *Cybersecurity Best Practices for the Safety of Modern Vehicles*.

title: Detecting correlated fleet cyber failures
subfield: Transportation data, cybersecurity, and benchmark infrastructure
open: Distinguish coordinated cyber compromise from common software defects, weather effects, or normal fleet behavior early enough to contain harm.
status: NHTSA emphasizes expanded attack surfaces and industrywide information sharing; reliable detection and response remain ongoing needs.
why: A common dependency can turn one weakness into simultaneous failures.
key_works: NHTSA (2024), *NHTSA/SAE Cybersecurity Workshop Keynote*.

title: Comparable cross-modal funding and performance data
subfield: Transportation data, cybersecurity, and benchmark infrastructure
open: Create maintained, comparable records linking revenues, subsidies, asset condition, service output, and outcomes across roads, transit, ports, and airports.
status: The 2024 National Academies appendix identifies major gaps in aggregated cross-modal financial and performance metrics.
why: Incompatible accounting obstructs rational comparisons and accountability.
key_works: National Academies (2024), *Critical Issues in Transportation for 2024 and Beyond*, research and metrics appendix.

title: Confidential freight data sharing
subfield: Transportation data, cybersecurity, and benchmark infrastructure
open: Support joint optimization and performance verification without exposing competitively sensitive customers, prices, capacities, or operating practices.
status: Shared logistics architectures need information exchange; commercial confidentiality remains a participation barrier.
why: Freight collaboration requires more than asking firms to publish their data.
key_works: Montreuil (2011), *Toward a Physical Internet*, DOI:10.1007/s12159-011-0045-x.

title: Prioritizing cyber defenses by physical consequence
subfield: Transportation data, cybersecurity, and benchmark infrastructure
open: Rank vulnerabilities and mitigations using credible physical safety consequences, including interacting failures, rather than software severity alone.
status: NHTSA’s research agenda explicitly raises criticality and standardized threat-analysis questions.
why: The most visible software weakness may not create the greatest physical risk.
key_works: NHTSA (2024), *NHTSA/SAE Cybersecurity Workshop Keynote*.

title: Representative disability mobility data with privacy
subfield: Transportation data, cybersecurity, and benchmark infrastructure
open: Collect sufficiently detailed longitudinal data to evaluate disability-specific barriers without exposing health status, routines, or sensitive destinations.
status: National surveys provide important population evidence; fine-grained longitudinal evaluation creates additional privacy and sampling challenges.
why: Small populations need both stronger representation and stronger protection.
key_works: BTS, *Travel Patterns of American Adults with Disabilities*; de Montjoye et al. (2013), *Unique in the Crowd*.

title: Fresh and contamination-resistant driving benchmarks
subfield: Transportation data, cybersecurity, and benchmark infrastructure
open: Maintain evaluation sets that detect training leakage, repeated test-set optimization, scenario aging, and geographic overfitting.
status: Large closed-loop benchmarks exist; fixed public benchmarks do not automatically remain independent evidence as models and datasets evolve.
why: Benchmark progress can otherwise reflect familiarity rather than safer driving.
key_works: Caesar et al. (2021), *nuPlan*, arXiv:2106.11810; Gulino et al. (2023), *Waymax*, arXiv:2310.08710.

title: Repurposed hydrogen-pipeline integrity
open: Predict safe operating envelopes for existing pipelines exposed to hydrogen, including welds, defects, fatigue, pressure cycling, and uncertain material histories.
status: Repurposing assessments identify important material and risk-model gaps; suitability cannot be inferred from original gas service alone.
why: Reuse could avoid major infrastructure construction only where integrity is established.
key_works: Yang et al. (2024), *Research gaps in quantitative risk assessment of hydrogen transmission pipelines*; Future Fuels CRC, *Review of future fuels transport and storage technologies*.

title: Empirical failure frequencies for hydrogen pipelines
open: Establish defensible incident-frequency and consequence models for new and repurposed hydrogen networks, including uncertainty from sparse operating experience.
status: Quantitative risk assessments remain constrained by limited hydrogen-specific incident and failure data.
why: Precise-looking risk calculations can conceal poorly supported event frequencies.
key_works: Yang et al. (2024), *Research gaps in quantitative risk assessment of hydrogen transmission pipelines*.

title: Repeatable microgravity cryogenic transfer
open: Demonstrate repeated propellant transfer with controlled vapor ingestion, chilldown loss, pressure, gauging, and coupling behavior under relevant microgravity conditions.
status: Mission studies and component development provide foundations; integrated repeatable transfer is a distinct operational requirement.
why: Enables reusable in-space transport and propellant depots.
key_works: Meyer et al. (2021), *Recent Concept Study for Cryogenic Fluid Management to Support Opposition Class Crewed Missions to Mars*, NASA NTRS 20210024129.

title: Long-duration low-loss cryogenic transport
open: Preserve usable cryogenic propellant over long missions while accounting for heat leaks, active cooling, power interruptions, slosh, and tank pressure.
status: Technology roadmaps identify coupled storage and transfer needs; component maturity does not establish complete mission reliability.
why: Propellant lost during waiting can dominate the mass budget of space logistics.
key_works: Stephens (2017), *Cryogenic Fluid Management Technology Development Roadmaps*, NASA NTRS 20170004449; Meyer et al. (2021), NTRS 20210024129.
